item.title: ‘What’s the Plan?’ Inside the Crisis Response at the Chi Phi House at Cornell
item.description:
The brothers of Chi Phi were texting one another in a panic.

On the afternoon of Nov. 8, 2024, Cornell University suspended the fraternity for suspected drug use. Three hours later, the school sent an email blast with the subject line, “Crime ALERT: Sexual Assault — Edgemoor Lane, City of Ithaca.”

It read: “The victim reported being sexually assaulted by several males and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.”

The Chi Phi house was indeed on Edgemoor Lane, and there was a night the brothers were worried about. But a simple detail in the email gave them fleeting hope.

“Dates don’t add up,” one man wrote to the other three brothers in the chat. Was the suspension notice referring maybe to a different Chi Phi party? Was that Risky Business Night? The more likely date the email was describing, they feared, was Oct. 19, 2024: Hawaiian Night, when things had gotten out of hand with a sorority sister.

“What’s the plan of action?” Matthew Ingalls, a sophomore studying math and economics, wrote. He had been in touch with the woman from Hawaiian Night several times since the party, text messages showed, and he had offered to call her again.

“I don’t think she would have reported this,” Mr. Ingalls offered to the group text.

He was wrong.

The woman, now known as Jane Doe, would go on to file a lawsuit describing a night at the Chi Phi house that began with a threesome with two of the brothers on the text chain but which was followed by sex acts with several other Chi Phi brothers. Those encounters, which Jane Doe said took place while she was incapacitated by ketamine and liquor, were, she later came to believe, a crime.

This article is based on a cache of documents collected during the university’s sexual assault investigation and obtained by The New York Times. Across more than 1,000 pages, the records paint a lurid picture of life inside the Tudor mansion of the Xi chapter of Chi Phi — one at odds with the “house on the hill,” as the fraternity’s website described it, that “still stands today as a monument to the ideals of brotherhood for which this chapter was founded.”

Judging from the lawsuit and even the accused brothers’ own statements, those ideals had warped and devolved inside that house on Hawaiian Night. And the events of that evening and the days that followed all played out over texts that were later submitted to investigators — texts seeming to invite anyone in the fraternity to join the brothers having sex with Jane Doe, and later ones urging calm as rumors spread.

In the wake of Hawaiian Night, the Chi Phi brothers seemed to have reason to believe that things might just return to normal. Various brothers reached out to Jane Doe with texts that sought to confirm everything was good.

“I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” one brother, Jonathan Newell, texted Jane Doe the following Monday, Oct. 21, 2024. He apologized repeatedly for being “too fucked up” to have prevented other Chi Phi brothers from entering the bedroom.

“We’ve been shutting down any stories we’ve heard,” he wrote. “But again I’m so so sorry.”

Jane Doe had gone to the party to see another brother, Mr. Ingalls, at the end of a very bad day. Someone had stolen her wallet while she was at the gym that afternoon, and she’d started drinking on an empty stomach and was already feeling a little drunk by the time she arrived at the Chi Phi house, she told investigators.

Mr. Ingalls had personally invited her to the party to “rip the Kraken,” the nickname for the fraternity’s bong, but soon after she’d arrived, he’d suggested a three-way, and in her drunken state, she’d agreed.

Now, days later, Mr. Ingalls sounded reassuring.

“It’ll blow over in a couple days I imagine,” he texted her. “Until then we just have to sit tight. How’ve you been coping with the stress? You need anything?”

But on private Chi Phi chats, the young men were worried about how the stories spreading on campus would affect them. As early as Sunday, there were rumblings among sororities and fraternities alike about a “gang bang” at Chi Phi.

“The talk of the town,” one of the seven men accused in Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Gillio Lopes, told investigators later. He said he had consensual sex with her that night.

“Most of the upperclassmen in the house mentioned it to me at one point or another that day,” Mr. Lopes said. “People just finding the situation relatively amusing.”

Over the next week and a half, Jane Doe’s own thinking about that night changed. Her sisters at Delta Delta Delta were alarmed by how she described what had happened that night, and bruises had formed on her buttocks. She was treated at the campus clinic for a urinary tract infection that she told the medical staff was contracted “in a traumatic way.”

But in her exchanges with the Chi Phi brothers, she seemed to be trying to move on.

“At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt,” she wrote to Mr. Newell, even as she fumed about what she felt was happening to her reputation. “i know im socially a massive slut rn and like can’t bare to hear it cuz im really not.”

But by the end of October, she was coming to believe that she had been a victim of sexual assault who was too incapacitated by alcohol and ketamine to be able to give consent. “I was raped,” she would flatly tell investigators.

There was a Halloween party planned at Chi Phi, and she’d said she planned to go until she got the sense that she had been uninvited.

“Yall aren’t my friends,” she texted Mr. Ingalls on Oct. 30, 2024. “Yall are covering your asses.”

Six days later, she went to the emergency room for a rape kit and then reported her sexual assault to the university.

“What’s the name of your lawyer,” Mr. Ingalls texted another brother three days after the email alert.

“I meeting him tmw,” the other man replied.

In the weeks that followed, several Chi Phi brothers named in the lawsuit were summoned before campus police officers and investigators with the university’s Title IX office, which is supposed to ensure compliance with federal civil rights laws.

Their versions of events that night, which often don’t line up with one another, matter-of-factly describe a room filling with men who, in their telling, have consensual sex in one form or another with the same woman. At least one brother gave his statement while his father listened virtually.

All the men have denied any wrongdoing and said that any sex that occurred that night was consensual. None of them have been charged with a crime.

The dozens of Chi Phi brothers living in the Chi Phi house most likely knew that they were under threat of eviction.

The Edgemoor Lane mansion, originally built in the 1800s on land owned by the family of Ezra Cornell himself, had a wood-paneled gallery with a fireplace and a bar where the parties took place. There was a large balcony where a D.J. could set up.

The upper floors, however, were a maze of rooms and hallways designed to accommodate the men who lived there. To the uninitiated, trying to get around could quickly become a confusing journey among various unconnected staircases.

Mr. Newell, a sophomore, shared a large bedroom with two brothers. But it was also a sort of common room in the house.

“It’s regularly used by brothers during events,” Mr. Newell later told investigators. “They just go in there, hang out, do whatever. We never lock the doors.”

This was where Jane Doe’s first sexual encounter happened that night, a threesome with Mr. Newell and Mr. Ingalls, which, according to her statement, she mistakenly presumed meant that they were bisexual, as she is.

Downstairs, the party was winding down. There were Chi Phi parties in the past that ended with people leaving in ambulances. This was not one of those parties.

“It was kind of like a ‘meh’ night,” one attendee recalled later in an interview with investigators.

Others would say the same thing about Chi Phi as a whole, which has been described as a “mid-tier” fraternity in the Greek landscape at Cornell.

Some friends and stragglers stuck around the house. Upstairs, a woman was vomiting in the fire staircase. The bartender — a sophomore studying information science named Winston Lee, who was assigned to remain sober that night — helped her get an Uber home.

The men’s accounts of that night have gaps within their details.

Mr. Newell recalled Mr. Ingalls noticing a bag of ketamine in his room and vaguely wondering how it got there — it was the second time that had happened lately, he told investigators. He took some and soon, he was vomiting in a trash can beside Mr. Ingalls.

Ketamine is a powerful and fast-acting anesthetic, rendering a dissociating or numbing effect on users for up to an hour or so, and unpredictable when combined with alcohol.

Mr. Newell described its effect on him to investigators: “I never really passed out. But there were pieces of my memory that I just can’t remember.” Mr. Ingalls eventually did pass out, and when Mr. Newell finished vomiting in a trash can, he looked up and saw that a third man, Mr. Lopes, a sophomore, had entered the room and was kissing Jane Doe. Soon, Mr. Lopes and Jane Doe were having sex. Mr. Ingalls woke up. “He was really confused,” Mr. Newell told investigators.

As this was happening, the door opened again, and “a couple other guys kind of poked their head in,” Mr. Newell recalled to investigators.

It is possible that these men had seen a Snapchat text sent from Mr. Newell’s account to a group of more than 50 fraternity brothers with an apparent invitation: “free pussy in alum pu,” meaning “pull up” to the alumni room upstairs, where Jane Doe was.

Mr. Ingalls followed up: “Like you can walk in and whip it out.”

Mr. Newell told investigators he didn’t remember sending or seeing any such texts.

Before the night ended, Jane Doe was led through the hallways to yet another room on an upper floor, where she eventually fell asleep. She woke up sometime around 10 a.m. in bed with Mr. Ingalls, who, according to her interview, asked for oral sex. She said no, and he drove her back to the Tri Delta house.

In the days that followed, the Chi Phi brothers appeared to make a plan.

“Just deny,” Mr. Newell recalled in his interview with investigators. “That was really it.”

After the fraternity was suspended in November, the Chi Phi house seems to have slowly cleared out as the semester wound down. All the brothers were told to find other housing.

“You know even if everything gets sorted before add/drop im withdrawing next semester,” Mr. Ingalls texted another of the seven fraternity brothers in January 2025, a little more than a week before the spring term would start.

“Yeah I figure this semester is cooked either way,” Mr. Lopes replied.

“Campus is gonna hate my ass for a while,” Mr. Ingalls responded, before turning to another upsetting development — his own brothers letting him down.

“Talking about ‘brotherhood’ and then no one except a couple real ones check in, much less acknowledge our existence,” Mr. Ingalls wrote.

“Dead ass bro,” came the reply.

Any code of silence seems to have eroded when the men were asked to voluntarily hand over screenshots of text exchanges about Hawaiian Night.

Scott Norris was a junior at Cornell at the time, and he showed up at his interview with investigators with a negative drug test for ketamine. “I’m excited to get this resolved,” he told them.

He had left the party, he said, and he was hanging out in an upper room with Scott Kretzschmar, a junior studying human biology. Then they saw the Snapchat message from Mr. Newell. Mr. Norris said he thought it might be a joke, but that he needed to see for himself.

“I was genuinely concerned and wanted to investigate what’s going on,” he said.

Mr. Norris and Mr. Kretzschmar, who was still wearing what he called “a Hawaiian necklace” from the party, entered the room where Jane Doe and four men were gathered. Satisfied that everything appeared “normal,” he told investigators, and nothing improper was happening, he and Mr. Kretzschmar left.

An investigator then showed him a screenshot from that “free pussy” text thread, in which he responded “Free…” and later, when someone asked, “Shop still open?” he responded “Yeah.”

Mr. Norris told investigators that the screenshot helped jog his memory. “I do now remember we were kind of just bantering about it in the chat, which I would never have done had I known what had actually gone on,” he said.

In the end, the men were given a range of punishments. Mr. Ingalls and Mr. Newell were expelled. Mr. Lee and Mr. Lopes received suspensions and disciplinary probation. Diego Sarabia, whom Jane Doe accused of forcibly kissing her and who had already graduated by the time of his punishment, was issued a persona non grata order, barring him from campus. Mr. Norris and Mr. Kretzschmar, who said they only stayed five minutes in the room, but who Jane Doe said had snorted ketamine off her body, were ordered to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention; they were also required to write “reflection papers.”

A Title IX investigator visited the Chi Phi house in January 2025. It was now vacant, months after the fraternity’s suspension in November.

The photographs the investigator took as she toured the house that day were included in the cache of documents obtained by The Times.

She photographed cigarette butts ground into a rug. A discarded condom in a wastebasket. Empty bags of snacks, empty beer cans, empty bottles. A bong.

A shelf with Narcan boxes. Beside them, protein powder.

In her own interview, Jane Doe thought back to the last moments before she, in effect, became Jane Doe, standing outside the Chi Phi house, excited to see Mr. Ingalls. She’d found him attractive.

She’d texted him to say she’d arrived, because she didn’t want to wait outside a frat house in the cold night to be let inside.

That, she said, “looks sad.”

Sharon Otterman, Troy Closson, Emma Goldberg, Debra Kamin, Hurubie Meko, Jonathan Baran, Amy Julia Harris, Alan Blinder, Maia Coleman, Nicole Hong, Duy Nguyen and Zach Seward contributed reporting.

item.title: Why Ketamine Immobilizes Some Users
item.description:
“The dose makes the poison,” as any toxicology student knows, describes the dangerously disparate effects that therapeutic compounds can have on health depending on the amount.

With many drugs — whether fentanyl, Tylenol or over-the-counter laxatives — the line between healing and harm is sometimes measured in milligrams. This principle is especially important when it comes to ketamine, the powerful anesthetic and party drug that has become increasingly popular as a mental health treatment.

Depending on the dose, ketamine in its powdered form can make a person feel pleasantly introspective, uncomfortably immobilized — or sedated enough to undergo surgery and not remember a thing.

The drug has been implicated in the case of a former Cornell University student who claimed in a lawsuit that she was raped by seven fraternity brothers during an hourslong attack. The student, identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe, said that she was already drunk when she arrived at the fraternity house and that the men pressured her to snort ketamine.

She told the police it was her first time trying the drug.

“Whenever the ketamine went down, I would say, is when things really start becoming a problem,” she later told university investigators.

The men have denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges have been filed against any of them.

For many health care providers, the case has drawn unflattering attention to a pharmaceutical workhorse that is valued for its efficacy, safety and predictability — when administered in a medical setting.

“Ketamine is one of those really interesting unicorns with a huge range of experiences and effects depending on the dose, the route of administration, the genetics of the patient and prior exposure,” said Dr. Brigitte Gordon, the clinical director at Journey Clinical, a chain of ketamine clinics.

A short-acting anesthetic, ketamine can have hallucinogenic effects at certain doses, and it can make users feel detached from pain and their surroundings.

Although considered safe when given in clinical settings, with chronic use it can cause serious bladder damage, cognitive impairment and a strong psychological dependency.

Mixing ketamine with alcohol or other drugs is especially dangerous, experts say. Both alcohol and ketamine depress the central nervous system. Together they can dangerously slow breathing, and cause cardiac problems and impaired cognition and coordination.

It is not clear how much ketamine Jane Doe snorted over the course of the evening, but she told investigators she did so repeatedly, in part to numb the anguish she said she was experiencing.

“I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out,” she told investigators. “My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with rape.”

The recreational use of ketamine has exploded in recent years, fueled in part by its easy availability via prescription and the therapeutic veneer associated with its use as an antidepressant.

In clinical settings, the drug is typically delivered intravenously or through injection, with doses ranging from 30 to 150 milligrams depending on a patient’s weight and previous use.

When given intravenously, the drug is released slowly, over the course of 40 or 60 minutes, and the patient’s vital signs are monitored throughout the session.

A modest, so-called psycholytic dose can prompt a dreamlike state and a shift in self-awareness, but patients are still conscious and able to speak.

Recreational users prefer the powdered form, because “giving yourself injections at a party is not very sexy,” said Dr. Steven Radowitz, the chief medical officer at Nushama, a chain of ketamine clinics.

Compared with its liquid form, powdered ketamine is far more portable. It is also highly concentrated. The amounts consumed in recreational settings can vary wildly, in part because the drug is seldom measured out with precision.

Dr. Sandhya Prashad, president of the American Society of Ketamine Physicians, Psychotherapists and Practitioners, said that recreational users sometimes snort more than a 1,000 milligrams at once — 10 times more than the dose used to treat depression.

“For someone who has never used ketamine before, a fairly small dose could send them into a K-hole,” she said, referring to the state of disassociation that leaves users nearly catatonic — awake but disconnected.

A K-hole seldom lasts for more than 45 minutes, but it leaves users highly vulnerable to abuse.

Given its numbing effects, ketamine might not seem to be a drug of choice for sexual activity. But Dr. Dave Rabin, a psychiatrist in New York who specializes in ketamine-assisted therapy, compared the drug’s dissociative effects with those of alcohol, which is often used to ease anxiety over intimacy.

Even then, he said, the dose matters. “Too much ketamine and a person’s judgment is impaired and they don’t have the agency to assert themselves,” he said.

Still, Dr. Rabin and other practitioners expressed concern that negative attention about ketamine could overshadow its therapeutic benefits. He said ketamine was unique as a fast-acting antidepressant that can interrupt suicidal thoughts and behavior with a single dose.

“Ketamine has tremendous utility when used and dosed properly,” he added. “As caregivers, the last thing we want is for powerful therapeutic tools like ketamine to to be classified as drugs of abuse.”
